steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on LeTI, a fine-tuning method that lets language models learn from textual feedback (like error messages from a Python interpreter) on code generation. Motivate the idea, explain how the method works, and summarize the main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Fine-tuning LMs with direct training signals; hypothesis about richer textual feedback
- LETI: idea and code-generation setting
- How LETI works
- Main results on code generation
- Textual vs. binary feedback; applicability to NLP tasks

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background and hypothesis
  - large-scale LMs shifted NLP paradigms; fine-tuning after pre-training on raw text crucial for benchmark tasks and aligning with human preferences
  - direct training signals: classification into right category, answering questions correctly, summarizing documents well, outputs aligned with human preferences
  - hypothesis: richer signals from textual interactions with environment (human, Python interpreter) - check correctness, pinpoint errors, explain why
- LETI idea
  - new LM fine-tuning paradigm: learn from nuanced textual interactions
  - evaluated on code generation (NL task description -> code)
  - natural, scalable automatic textual feedback: stack traces, error messages from PL tools e.g. Python interpreter
  - mirrors software development cycle: write, execute, improve until satisfying (no error); developer learns from mistakes, becomes (slightly) better
  - evidence LETI learns from past mistakes (§ 3.2)
- Method
  - base LM pre-trained on natural language and code generates program from NL instruction; tested on test cases
  - fine-tune on concatenation of instruction, generated program, textual feedback (only when program fails)
  - prepend reward token (binary feedback): <|good|> vs <|bad|>; condition on <|good|> to generate correct solutions
  - multiple rounds; no instruction-code paired data
- Results
  - MBPP, no ground-truth code
  - 63.2% more syntactically correct, executable code (2B LM) vs pre-trained, no post-processing
  - with post-processing: eliminates most NameError issues (10% -> 1% on 2B LM) in two iterations
  - generalizes to HumanEval (§ 3.2)
  - no cost to original capability (reasoning, chain-of-thought) thanks to continued pre-training auxiliary objective (§ 3.4)
- Textual vs binary feedback; NLP tasks
  - textual feedback: better performance, more sample efficient, about half the gradient steps for same performance, 2B model (§ 3.3)
  - also applies to NLP tasks (event argument extraction) formulated as code generation (§ 3.5)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale language models have fundamentally changed the paradigms of natural language processing (NLP). LMs are pre-trained on raw text, and the fine-tuning stages after that have proven crucial for improving their capabilities in solving benchmark NLP tasks and in generating texts that align with human preferences. Success has come from fine-tuning with direct training signals that measure whether the model, e.g., puts the input into the right category, answers a question correctly, summarizes documents well, and generates outputs that align with human preferences. We hypothesize that LMs can use much richer training signals from textual interactions with the environment (e.g., a human or a Python interpreter), which do not only check whether the LM's outputs are correct but also pinpoint the errors and explain why.

We propose LETI, a new LM fine-tuning paradigm that explores the potential of LMs to learn from nuanced textual interactions. We evaluate LETI on code generation tasks, where the LM has to generate code pieces to solve tasks described in natural language. In this setting there is a natural and scalable way to get automatic interactive textual feedback: the stack traces and error messages output by established programming language (PL) tools such as a Python interpreter. The way LETI improves is like a typical software development cycle: a human developer writes an initial program, runs it, and improves the program based on the feedback from the programming environment until a satisfying solution is found (e.g., it runs successfully with no error). The human developer also learns from the mistakes made in this process and becomes a (slightly) better developer who can avoid similar mistakes in the future. Similarly, we give empirical evidence that LETI can learn from past mistakes and avoid similar errors in § 3.2.

- Method: base LM (natural language + code) generates program from NL instruction, tested on test cases; fine-tune on instruction + generated program + textual feedback (only on failure); reward token prepended, <|good|> vs <|bad|>; multiple rounds; no instruction-code paired data
- Results: MBPP, no ground-truth code; 63.2% more syntactically correct/executable code (2B), no post-processing; with post-processing NameError 10% -> 1% in two iterations; generalizes to HumanEval (§ 3.2); original capability (reasoning, chain-of-thought) kept via continued pre-training objective (§ 3.4)
- Textual vs binary feedback: better performance, about half the gradient steps for 2B model (§ 3.3); also works for NLP tasks like event argument extraction as code generation (§ 3.5)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale language models have fundamentally changed the paradigms of natural language processing (NLP). LMs are pre-trained on raw text, and the fine-tuning stages after that have proven crucial for improving their capabilities in solving benchmark NLP tasks and in generating texts that align with human preferences. Success has come from fine-tuning with direct training signals that measure whether the model, e.g., puts the input into the right category, answers a question correctly, summarizes documents well, and generates outputs that align with human preferences. We hypothesize that LMs can use much richer training signals from textual interactions with the environment (e.g., a human or a Python interpreter), which do not only check whether the LM's outputs are correct but also pinpoint the errors and explain why.

We propose LETI, a new LM fine-tuning paradigm that explores the potential of LMs to learn from nuanced textual interactions. We evaluate LETI on code generation tasks, where the LM has to generate code pieces to solve tasks described in natural language. In this setting there is a natural and scalable way to get automatic interactive textual feedback: the stack traces and error messages output by established programming language (PL) tools such as a Python interpreter. The way LETI improves is like a typical software development cycle: a human developer writes an initial program, runs it, and improves the program based on the feedback from the programming environment until a satisfying solution is found (e.g., it runs successfully with no error). The human developer also learns from the mistakes made in this process and becomes a (slightly) better developer who can avoid similar mistakes in the future. Similarly, we give empirical evidence that LETI can learn from past mistakes and avoid similar errors in § 3.2.

In LETI, a base LM that was pre-trained on both natural language and code is asked to generate a program conditioned on the natural language instruction, and then the program is tested on a suite of test cases. LETI fine-tunes the model on a concatenation of the natural language instruction, the program generated by the LM, and the textual feedback (e.g., stack traces and error messages) that pinpoints the bug, which is only given when the generated program fails to solve the task. Besides the textual feedback, we also put a reward token (i.e., binary feedback) at the start of the fine-tuning sequences. It is different for correct (<|good|>) and buggy solutions (<|bad|>), which encourages the LM to generate correct solutions when it is conditioned on <|good|>. LETI repeats this procedure for multiple rounds, and during this iterative process LETI does not assume any instruction-code paired data.

We find that LETI improves the performance of the LM on code generation tasks in MBPP without using any ground-truth code. Specifically, it generates 63.2\% more syntactically correct and executable code (on the 2B LM) than the pre-trained model, without any of the commonly used post-processing heuristics. When post-processing is used, LETI (2B) improves performance and gets rid of most NameError issues, which happen when a variable or function is not defined (from 10% to 1% on the 2B LM), in two iterations. The optimized LM also shows a general performance improvement on another code generation dataset, HumanEval (§ 3.2). This improvement on in-domain tasks does not cost the capabilities of the original LM (e.g., reasoning and chain-of-thought capability), because LETI has an auxiliary objective that continues pre-training (§ 3.4).

We see that textual feedback is better for improving the LM than baselines that only use binary feedback. It gives better performance and better sample efficiency, needing only about half of the gradient steps to reach the same performance for the 2B-scale model (§ 3.3). We also find that LETI can be applied just as well to NLP tasks (e.g., event argument extraction) when they can be formulated as code generation problems (§ 3.5).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale language models have fundamentally shifted the paradigms of natural language processing (NLP). Based on LMs pre-trained on raw text, subsequent fine-tuning stages have proven crucial to enhance their capabilities in solving benchmark NLP tasks and generating texts that align with human preferences. Success has been achieved by fine-tuning with direct training signals that measure whether the model, e.g., classifies the input into the right category [2], answers a question correctly [3,4], summarizes documents well [5,6], and generates outputs that align with human preferences [7,8]. We hypothesize that LMs can harness much richer training signals from textual interactions with the environment (e.g., a human or a Python interpreter) that not only check the correctness of the LM's outputs but also pinpoint the errors and explain why.

We propose LETI, a new LM fine-tuning paradigm that aims to explore LMs' potential to learn from nuanced textual interactions. We evaluate LETI on code generation tasks, where the LM is supposed to generate code pieces to solve tasks described in natural language. This setting invites a natural and scalable way to acquire automatic interactive textual feedback: the stack traces and error messages output by established programming language (PL) tools such as a Python interpreter. LETI's improvement process mirrors a typical software development cycle: a human developer writes an initial program, executes it, and improves the program based on feedback obtained from the programming environment until a satisfying solution is found (e.g., successfully executed with no error); furthermore, the human developer learns from mistakes in this process and becomes a (slightly) better developer who can avoid similar mistakes in the future. Similarly to the human development process, we provide empirical evidence that LETI can learn from past mistakes and avoid similar errors in § 3.2.

In LETI, a base LM pre-trained on both natural language and code is asked to generate a program conditioned on the natural language instruction, which is then tested on a suite of test cases. LETI fine-tunes the model on a concatenation of the natural language instruction, the LM-generated program, and the textual feedback (e.g., stack traces and error messages) that pinpoints the bug, which is only provided when the generated program fails to solve the task. In addition to textual feedback, we prepend the fine-tuning sequences with a reward token (i.e., binary feedback), which differs for correct (<|good|>) and buggy solutions (<|bad|>), to encourage the LM to generate correct solutions when conditioned on <|good|>. LETI repeats this procedure for multiple rounds, and during this iterative process it assumes no instruction-code paired data.

We find that LETI improves the LM's performance on code generation tasks in MBPP [1] without using any ground-truth code. Specifically, it generates 63.2\% more syntactically correct and executable code (on the 2B LM) compared to the pre-trained model, without any commonly employed post-processing heuristics. When post-processing is applied, LETI (2B) improves performance and eliminates most NameError issues that occur when a variable or function is not defined (from 10% to 1% on the 2B LM) in two iterations. The optimized LM also shows a generalized performance improvement on another code generation dataset, HumanEval [13] (§ 3.2). This improvement on in-domain tasks does not come at the cost of the capabilities of the original LM (e.g., reasoning and chain-of-thought capability [14]), thanks to LETI's auxiliary objective of continued pre-training (§ 3.4).

We observe that textual feedback is advantageous for improving the LM compared to baselines that only use binary feedback, as it offers enhanced performance and greater sample efficiency, requiring only about half of the gradient steps to reach the same performance for the 2B-scale model (§ 3.3). Furthermore, we find that LETI is equally applicable to NLP tasks (e.g., event argument extraction [15]) when they can be formulated as code generation problems (§ 3.5).
